name: Hair dye and bleaching
lead: Hair dye and bleaching change the color of head hair. People use them to cover gray, to match hair to a skin tone or style, or to shift contrast, for example dyeing hair a darker shade or bleaching it lighter. Looksmaxxing forum members discuss both as a way to change how the hair frames the face, and also use dye on brows, lashes and facial hair.[1][2][3]

Bleaching lightens hair by oxidizing melanin, typically with hydrogen peroxide and an alkaline agent such as ammonia.[1] Dyes deposit color in or on the hair shaft. Permanent dyes use an oxidizing developer, while semi-permanent and temporary dyes stain the hair without lightening it.[1][4] Dye use is widespread: reports cited by Wikipedia say 50 to 80 percent of women in the US, Europe and Japan have used it, and US at-home coloring sales were reported at $4.8 billion in 2024.[1]

The practice is among the oldest cosmetic techniques on record, with dye recipes in Assyrian and Egyptian texts, and the modern synthetic industry dates to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.[1] A cultural layer sits on top of the chemistry: blond, dark and red hair carry different associations in different eras, and studies of hair color and attractiveness have reported mixed or context-dependent preferences.[15]

Documented downsides include scalp irritation, allergy to p-phenylenediamine (PPD), breakage and unexpected tones. The US National Cancer Institute describes research on personal hair dye use and cancer as mixed, and the FDA says it has no reliable evidence linking current coal-tar hair dyes to cancer while it continues to monitor the research.[1][4][12]

angle.text: Color is a direct visual change: gray is covered, a pale or ginger shade can be taken to black or dark brown, and dark hair can be lightened. Forum users ask about colors that match their wet or natural hair, or what shade suits their complexion, and use dye to even out patchy brows and beards.

paras: Hair color is set by melanin in the cortex of the hair shaft. Coloring products either remove or alter that pigment (bleach), add pigment (dye), or do both in one step (permanent color with a lightening developer). The look people aim for ranges from invisible gray coverage to a deliberate change of shade, such as natural dark brown to platinum or ginger to black.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing and grooming discussion the appeal is contrast and framing. Hair that is darker or lighter than the skin changes how the face reads, and dye on brows, lashes or beard can make them look fuller or more even. Members ask which shade matches how their hair looks when wet, or which dark tone suits their complexion.[3][8]

Permanent dye uses ammonia and an oxidizing developer to open the hair cuticle and form pigment in the cortex. The National Cancer Institute notes that permanent products make up about 80 percent of those marketed and work by reacting colorless intermediates with hydrogen peroxide.[4] Wikipedia describes the three components as a primary intermediate, a coupler and an oxidant, and says permanence comes from large dye molecules forming inside and being trapped in the hair.[1]

Demi-permanent dye uses a lower peroxide level and cannot lighten hair, fading over roughly 20 to 28 shampoos. Semi-permanent dye lasts about 4 to 8 shampoos, and temporary products wash out in one shampoo.[1] Vivid or fashion colors contain tint but no developer, so on dark hair they usually require bleaching first.[1]

Plant dyes form a separate category. Henna was used in ancient Egypt and the Near East and gives orange to auburn tones, with indigo blended in for browns and blacks. A product sold as black henna may instead contain PPD, which is a different and much more allergenic substance.[14]

Bleaching breaks down melanin by oxidation, releasing oxygen gas. Bleached hair can turn brassy or yellow, and toners and purple shampoos are used to correct undertones.[1] Home bleaching products typically contain about 6 percent hydrogen peroxide, and salon products up to 12 percent.[1]

A looksmax.org poster who bleached already light-blond hair reported that it reached near-white after toning and showed little visible regrowth, while another member in the same thread said bleach is permanent but can leave hair in poor texture for people who start dark and need long processing.[5]
The word bleaching is also used for skin and tooth lightening; these are separate practices covered in their own entries.

Wikipedia lists on-scalp methods such as all-over color, root touch-ups, typically needed every 4 to 6 weeks, and block coloring, and off-scalp methods such as highlights, lowlights, ombre and balayage, where color is hand-painted onto sections.[1]

Regrowth is a recurring practical point: as hair grows, the line between natural and dyed hair shows, which is why root touch-ups recur on a schedule. One looksmax.org poster reported little visible regrowth after bleaching already light hair.[1][5]

Hair dye recipes appear in Assyrian herbals from about 2177 BCE, and the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) describes dyeing gray hair. Assyrian tablets from the seventh century BCE describe darkening gray hair with plant and animal ingredients, and Diodorus Siculus described Celtic peoples bleaching hair with lime.[1] A mummy of the 17th Dynasty, Ahmose-Henuttamehu, has been reported with hair dyed red, probably with henna.[14]

In the nineteenth century henna became fashionable in Europe among artistic circles, and William Henry Perkin's accidental discovery of mauveine in 1856 launched synthetic dyes. The reactivity of para-phenylenediamine was identified in the 1860s, Eugene Schueller is credited with the first synthetic hair dye in 1907, and Schwarzkopf launched a home color product in 1947.[1][14] The NCI reports that manufacturers changed permanent dye formulas in the mid to late 1970s to remove some intermediates found to be carcinogenic in animals.[4]

Bleached blond hair has its own history: Wikipedia traces blond associations from ancient Greece and Rome through to Anita Loos's 1925 novel Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, and cites a 2007 French study that found about 20 percent of women were blonde, roughly half of them artificially.[15]

Threads on looksmax.org include members asking how to dye hair while limiting damage, how to go from ginger to black, and which dark shade matches the look of their hair when wet.[2][3][6] Other threads discuss dyeing brows, lashes and facial hair, and how to judge whether black or dark brown will suit a complexion.[7][8]

The questions are typically practical and about matching: whether a shade suits skin undertone and eye color, whether dye hides thinning or patchiness, and how bleached hair holds up. Hacker News discussions of health studies show a separate audience that approaches hair dye from a risk perspective.[10][11]

Studies cited by Wikipedia on hair color and attraction have produced mixed results. Some found no general Western male preference for blondes, a 2008 study of men in Greater London preferred dark-haired women, and a 2018 University of Florida student study found a preference for brunettes. Researchers have proposed that dark hair may dominate fashion and modeling or be perceived as healthier.[15]
No study has tested hair color change as a deliberate way to improve attractiveness, so claims about particular shades rest on personal reports and fashion convention.[1]

The EU is described as especially strict: Directive 2012/21/EU restricts about 45 chemicals in hair dyes.[1] In the US, coal-tar hair dyes are exempt from color additive pre-approval but must carry a caution statement and skin-test directions, and the FDA states that eyebrow and eyelash dyeing are not permitted uses of coal-tar hair dyes because injuries including blindness have occurred.[12] The FDA also repealed its approval of lead acetate in hair dyes, effective January 6, 2022.[12]

Dye can cause skin irritation, allergic reactions, hair breakage and skin staining. PPD-based dyes have been controversial, symptoms can appear hours to a day later, and manufacturers recommend patch testing, which some European dermatologists advise against for self-testing.[1] The FDA recommends repeating the test before every use, says PPD is the ingredient most often linked to reactions, and notes that sensitization can build with repeated exposure.[12]

PPD sensitization is described as lasting for life, and temporary black henna tattoos containing PPD have been linked to severe reactions and later reactions to hair dye. Wikipedia reports PPD was the tenth most common allergen in patch tests in 2005 to 2006, and the American Contact Dermatitis Society named it Allergen of the Year in 2006.[13][14]

In 2010 the International Agency for Research on Cancer classed some chemicals encountered by hairdressers as probably carcinogenic, while personal hair dye use was judged not classifiable. The NCI describes results for bladder cancer, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and breast cancer as mixed or inconsistent; for breast cancer it cites a large US cohort in which users had a 1.07 times higher risk among non-Hispanic White women and 1.45 times among Black women, with some data suggesting home dyers may have higher risk than those dyed professionally.[4] Wikipedia also cites a 2017 meta-analysis reporting about 20 percent higher breast cancer risk among users.[1] A 2024 case report in JAMA Ophthalmology described retinopathy associated with hair dye.[9]

No studies found testing hair color change as a means of improving attractiveness. Epidemiological studies on hair dye use and health include the Copenhagen City Heart Study (2016, 7,684 women followed for 37 years) and a 2018 meta-analysis on breast cancer risk.[1] The NCI summarizes a 2014 pooled analysis of 17 studies that found no increased bladder cancer risk with personal use, a 2010 meta-analysis of 42 studies finding nearly twice the bladder cancer risk in hairdressers working at least 10 years, and a 2020 cohort that found no association with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.[4] Studies of dental bleaching, found in the same literature, concern teeth rather than hair.

Related entries include eyebrow and lash tinting, hair loss concealment, and the style and grooming practices that shape how hair frames the face. Chemical straighteners, which some studies group with dyes in cancer research, are a separate product class.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hair dye and bleach come up as practical questions about shade choice, damage and how to lighten or darken hair, while external health coverage focuses on allergy and cancer studies.[2][3][5]

claims.claim: Bleaching works best on already light hair
claims.believers: A member reports that his light-blond hair went near-white after toning with little visible regrowth, while those starting dark get harsher texture.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that vivid colors on dark hair usually require bleaching first, and that bleached hair can turn brassy and need toning.[1]

claims.claim: Dyeing to a darker shade can improve how the face looks
claims.believers: Posters ask for the dark brown or black that matches their hair when wet, saying it looks better than their dry natural color.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested whether hair color change affects attractiveness; studies of hair color preference report mixed results.[1][15]

claims.believers: Hacker News threads discussed a 2019 study linking permanent dye to breast cancer.[10][11]
claims.experts: The NCI describes evidence on personal use as mixed, with some studies suggesting small increases for certain cancers and others finding none; the FDA says it has no reliable evidence linking current coal-tar hair dyes to cancer.[4][12]

claims.claim: Natural dyes such as henna are a gentler alternative to chemical dye
claims.believers: Plant dyes are traditional in the Near East and South Asia and are chosen by people who want to avoid ammonia and synthetic dyes.[14]
claims.experts: Henna itself is not the cause of the severe reactions seen with black henna; those are attributed to added PPD, and neutral or black products can differ from true henna.[14]

claims.claim: Brows and lashes can be dyed at home like head hair
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread says hair dye works for eyebrows, lashes and facial hair.[7]
claims.experts: The FDA states that eyebrow and eyelash dyeing are not permitted uses of coal-tar hair dyes and that dyes near the eyes have caused injuries including blindness.[12]

claims.claim: A patch test beforehand predicts whether a reaction will happen
claims.believers: Manufacturers and the FDA recommend a skin test before use.[12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that European dermatologists advise against self-testing, arguing it can cause sensitization and be misread; the FDA says a clear result is not a guarantee.[1][12]

claims.claim: Blond hair makes women more attractive
claims.believers: The idea is widespread in popular culture, including Anita Loos's 1925 novel.[15]
claims.experts: Studies cited by Wikipedia found no general Western male preference for blondes, with some samples favoring dark hair.[15]

card.summary: Bleaching or dyeing hair to change contrast; well-established cosmetic method with allergy and damage risks.
card.note: PPD allergy, breakage and unexpected color are documented; cancer-risk studies are inconsistent.

quick.overview:
Hair dye and bleach change hair color, and in style circles they are discussed as a way to change contrast, such as lighter or darker hair.

Coloring is common and the techniques are well established, but no studies test whether it improves attractiveness. Documented risks include irritation, allergy and breakage.
quick.mechanism: Permanent dye and bleach use an oxidizer and alkaline agent to open the hair cuticle; bleach oxidizes melanin, while dye deposits color. Lower-strength dyes coat or lightly penetrate the hair without lightening.
quick.risks: Reported risks are skin irritation, PPD allergy, hair damage and skin staining. Studies linking dye to cancer are limited and inconsistent. The EU restricts about 45 hair dye chemicals.
